criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to a municipal drinking-water watermain extension for 64 homes on Senanus Drive in Central Saanich (British Columbia, Canada) relying on contaminated and seasonally depleted private wells.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines municipal governance, institutional conflict, regional-versus-municipal jurisdiction, and municipal engineering decision-making around watermain extension. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study empirically examines concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing watermain connection and exclusion: (1) municipal land-use/zoning rules (RE-3 rural estate zoning lot-size rules and Official Community Plan bylaws) and an explicit municipal waterline-extension policy withholding piped water to prevent rural subdivision/development; (2) cost-recovery and petition threshold rules governing resident-funded extensions (requiring 50% of properties representing two-thirds of land value under the petition method, council rejection of a fully resident-funded extension, cost-recovery feasibility criteria for extension applications, assessment-based cost allocation, and federal-provincial-municipal grant cost-sharing); and (3) statutory/bylaw administrative discretion (Bylaw No. 1410 granting the municipal engineer sole discretion over the diameter and location of every water service connection) and regional-versus-municipal jurisdictional rules.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative anthropological empirical evidence from a 10-year case study drawing on 22 stakeholder and resident interviews, audio recordings of public meetings, minutes of municipal council, committee, and regional district meetings, Water Advisory Task Force majority/minority reports, well logs, and technical/health assessments.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete service access, exclusion, availability, quantity, quality, and affordability/cost outcomes: 30 years of exclusion from the municipal watermain for 64 homes, defeated motions for resident-funded connection, household coping (driving 4-5 km to gas stations for 20 L water containers, hauled water, multiple wells, inadequate drought/fire storage), and eventual policy approval (2005) and CAD 1,600,000 intergovernmental grant funding (2007) for the watermain extension.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and units of analysis (64 unserviced rural-estate households/properties along Senanus Drive and Mount Newton Cross Road in the District of Central Saanich, BC, plus municipal institutions and 22 interviewed stakeholders), rule-type legal/administrative exposures, access/exclusion outcomes, and qualitative longitudinal anthropological case-study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: Municipal engineers were asked to write reports and summarise other reports for the purpose of informing the municipal council on whether to extend the existing watermain by 4 km to service 64 homes currently drawing their water from wells (many of which had shown, in some tests, high biological and chemical contaminant levels).

However, Central Saanich town councils and mayors blocked all demands, attempting to keep the watermain away from Senanus Drive to prevent the area from being developed, as one of the mayors told local newspapers while in ofﬁce.

The diameter and location of every water service connection being at the sole discretion of the municipal engineer (bylaw no. 1410), engineering staff had to make a decision concerning the size of the supply line.

Strategies, including ‘working on those who do not need the watermain’, would be easier to impede with the 50% of the properties representing two-thirds of the land value requirement (under the petition method) for adopting a resident-funded watermain.

This study of the conﬂict around water is based on a large number of documents, including all newspaper articles, minutes of municipal and district meetings, all scientiﬁc and task force reports submitted to the municipal engineering department, 22 interviews with the major players and residents involved (including the mayor, chair of water and waste management committee), audio recordings of public meetings, records of the meetings and documents produced by the Water Advisory Task Force (WATF), well logs, scientiﬁc, medical and engineering reports, personal notes kept by a person working for the WATF chair, and minutes of the water and waste management committee.

The nearest gas stations where residents collected water during periods of high water contamination levels in 20 l (5 gallon) containers (as photographically depicted in one newspaper article) are in Brentwood and Saanichton, meaning that residents had to drive 4–5 km each way to obtain drinking water.

raw_response.exposure: Municipal waterline-extension and anti-development zoning policy (RE-3 rural estate zoning and Official Community Plan land-use bylaws), cost-recovery and petition threshold rules (50% of properties representing two-thirds of land value requirement under the petition method; cost-recovery feasibility criteria), municipal engineer discretion over service connections (Bylaw No. 1410), and municipal-versus-regional water jurisdiction.
raw_response.outcome: Household and community connection/exclusion from the municipal drinking-water watermain (30-year denial of watermain extension, defeat of resident-funded extension motion, reliance on contaminated/low-yield private wells and hauled water from gas stations, and subsequent 2005 policy approval and 2007 CAD 1.6 million grant-funded extension approval).
raw_response.population_and_sample: 64 unserviced rural-zoned households/properties on Senanus Drive and Mount Newton Cross Road in the District of Central Saanich, Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada; empirical dataset comprises 22 interviews with residents and municipal actors plus extensive municipal, task-force, health, and public-meeting records over a 10-year period.
raw_response.rationale: This 10-year qualitative anthropological case study empirically examines household and community access to a municipal drinking-water watermain extension in Central Saanich, Canada, satisfying all inclusion criteria (c1-c6) under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Specifically, it documents how municipal waterline-extension and rural-zoning policies (RE-3 zoning and land-use bylaws), petition voting/land-value thresholds (50% of properties representing two-thirds of land value) and cost-recovery rules for extensions, municipal engineer discretion under Bylaw No. 1410, and municipal-versus-regional jurisdiction directly governed 30 years of household exclusion from piped municipal water and eventual approval. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are explicitly eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative longitudinal anthropological case study (interviews, public-meeting audio transcripts, and archival/documentary analysis)
